bibl.title: Cooperative Subnetworks of Molecularly Similar Interneurons in Mouse Neocortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether members of a molecularly defined interneuron class fire together as a population rather than individually, and what circuit mechanisms would make that happen
span.quote: Here we show in vivo and in vitro that members of two non-overlapping neocortical IN populations, expressing somatostatin (SOM) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), are active as populations rather than individually. We demonstrate a variety of synergistic mechanisms, involving population-specific local excitation, GABAergic disinhibition and excitation through electrical coupling, which likely underlie IN population co-activity. Firing of a few SOM or VIP INs recruits additional members within the cell type via GABAergic and cholinergic mechanisms, thereby amplifying the output of the population as a whole.

span.label: how interneurons coordinate their activity within a subpopulation, given that the populations inhibit each other and sit in a densely interconnected network
span.quote: However, it is unclear how interneurons coordinate their activity within subpopulations. It is particularly puzzling how mutually inhibitory interneuron populations manage to operate together while embedded within a highly interconnected network.

span.label: four complementary mechanisms that recruit members of the same interneuron class, and a proposal to replace the hierarchical model with reciprocally inhibitory population dyads
span.quote: We therefore propose an updated standard model for IN connectivity in the neocortex featuring reciprocally inhibitory population dyads rather than sequential hierarchy of populations and groups rather than individual neurons as computational units

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We demonstrate a variety of synergistic mechanisms, involving population-specific local excitation, GABAergic disinhibition and excitation through electrical coupling, which likely underlie IN population co-activity.

span.label: within-population co-activity of neocortical interneurons
span.quote: Here we show in vivo and in vitro that members of two non-overlapping neocortical IN populations, expressing somatostatin (SOM) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), are active as populations rather than individually.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To probe this directly, we used multi-cell patch clamp to assess connectivity parameters between nearby (intersomatic distances 20–100 µm) PCs and VIPs or SOMs in triple-transgenic VIP-cre∷LSL-TOM∷SOM-GFP(GIN) slices (see Methods).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Four converging circuit mechanisms recruit members of the same interneuron class: electrical coupling, absent or scarce within-population inhibition, disinhibition via inhibition of the reciprocally inhibitory class, and cholinergic self-excitation of VIPs.
span.quote: Our data suggest that VIPs and SOMs recruit their population members through four mechanisms: electrical coupling, complete lack (SOMs) or relative scarcity (VIPs) of within-population inhibition (see also ( Hu et al., 2011 , Ma et al., 2012 )), strong within-population disinhibition through inhibition of the reciprocally inhibitory population, and self-excitation of VIPs via ACh release.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: VIPs inhibiting SOMs (and vice versa) removes inhibition from their own population members, so firing in a few cells raises the co-activity of the whole population.
span.quote: Through the inhibitory synapses between VIPs and SOMs, these INs can disinhibit members of the same population, effectively increasing the co-activity of the population.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Acetylcholine produced by VIPs recruits further VIPs that are themselves ACh-sensitive, closing a positive feedback loop.
span.quote: The recruitment of VIPs by exogenous ACh ( Figure S6 ) and their mecamylamine-sensitive population-recruitment ( Figure 5H ), combined with their ability to produce ACh ( von Engelhardt et al., 2007 ) suggest that ambient ACh recruits a positive feedback loop via VIPs.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Strongly facilitating, slow-kinetics inhibitory synapses between SOMs and VIPs grow during sustained firing, sustaining disinhibition of the partner population over hundreds of milliseconds.
span.quote: Facilitating synapses are ideal for promoting activity of population members on >100 ms timescales through inhibition of a reciprocally connected inhibitory population (see next section).

span.label: four mechanisms recruit members of the same class: electrical coupling, absent or scarce within-population inhibition, disinhibition through the reciprocally inhibitory population, and self-excitation of VIPs
span.quote: Our data suggest that VIPs and SOMs recruit their population members through four mechanisms: electrical coupling, complete lack (SOMs) or relative scarcity (VIPs) of within-population inhibition (see also ( Hu et al., 2011 , Ma et al., 2012 )), strong within-population disinhibition through inhibition of the reciprocally inhibitory population, and self-excitation of VIPs via ACh release.

span.label: and a fifth from outside: the surrounding excitatory network drives each population with its own synaptic dynamics, depressing onto VIPs and facilitating onto SOMs
span.quote: PCs formed excitatory synapses onto VIPs and SOMs at similar rates, but synapses onto VIPs were depressing, while those onto SOMs were facilitating ( Figure 2A ). Additional recordings in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) also demonstrated a depressing synaptic PC->VIP connection (5/38 connections, 13%) suggesting that the organization of SOM versus VIP excitation dynamics is conserved across sensory cortices.

span.label: the recruitment of VIPs by exogenous ACh and their mecamylamine-sensitive population-recruitment, combined with their ability to produce ACh, suggest that ambient ACh recruits a positive feedback loop via VIPs
span.quote: The recruitment of VIPs by exogenous ACh ( Figure S6 ) and their mecamylamine-sensitive population-recruitment ( Figure 5H ), combined with their ability to produce ACh ( von Engelhardt et al., 2007 ) suggest that ambient ACh recruits a positive feedback loop via VIPs.

span.label: separating the excitatory sources of two mutually inhibitory populations is likened to agonist and antagonist muscles, where contracting both at once would waste energy
span.quote: The situation is similar to motor coordination of agonist/antagonist muscle pairs where simultaneous contraction of both would not be energetically advantageous. Along this line of reasoning, it would make sense to segregate PC networks to feed only into one population of a mutually inhibitory pair of IN populations. Our data in Figures 3 and S3 support this hypothesis in the case of SOMs and VIPs.

span.label: the proposed function is supralinear amplification of one kind of inhibition as demand grows, for instance before excitation overwhelms the circuit
span.quote: IN population cooperativity may be advantageous to circuit operation by predictively amplifying the particular type of inhibition (dendrite targeting, perisomatic or disinhibitory) provided by the population. Thus these multiple cooperative specializations would operate together to deliver wider-spread and increased inhibition in a supralinear proportion to growing demand, for example when excitation is about to overwhelm the circuit and cause epilepsy.

span.label: The proposed mechanisms are supported mostly by correlation because the cell-type-specific loss-of-function tools needed do not exist.
span.quote: We note however that as suitable loss-of-function experiments to test the contribution of these mechanisms to IN population co-activity do not yet exist (synaptic blockers simultaneously specific to both pre- and postsynaptic populations would be necessary), our data mostly imply the involvement of these mechanisms by correlation rather than directly.

span.label: Broad optogenetic activation also stimulates axon terminals, so the recruitment results may reflect complex network interactions rather than direct drive.
span.quote: This broad activation of the local microcircuit includes axon terminals expressing C1V1, therefore these results may be due to multiple complex network interactions among the excitatory and inhibitory cell types.

span.label: The marker-defined populations probably contain finer subpopulations that were not resolved here.
span.quote: While the IN populations can be conveniently categorized by the non-overlapping markers SOM, PV and VIP to utilize transgenic mice, we note that there are likely further subpopulations within these that should fit the cooperativity/co-activity framework described here on average for these broad populations.

span.label: the mechanisms are implied by correlation rather than shown directly, because the loss-of-function reagent that would be needed does not exist
span.quote: We note however that as suitable loss-of-function experiments to test the contribution of these mechanisms to IN population co-activity do not yet exist (synaptic blockers simultaneously specific to both pre- and postsynaptic populations would be necessary), our data mostly imply the involvement of these mechanisms by correlation rather than directly.

span.label: broad optogenetic activation also excites axon terminals, so those results may reflect complex network interactions
span.quote: This broad activation of the local microcircuit includes axon terminals expressing C1V1, therefore these results may be due to multiple complex network interactions among the excitatory and inhibitory cell types.

span.label: the three marker classes are convenient rather than fundamental, and the framework is expected to hold on average for populations known to contain further subtypes
span.quote: While the IN populations can be conveniently categorized by the non-overlapping markers SOM, PV and VIP to utilize transgenic mice, we note that there are likely further subpopulations within these that should fit the cooperativity/co-activity framework described here on average for these broad populations. Although we did not find subdivisions that correlate with consistent differences in electrophysiological parameters ( Figure S5 ), other metrics such as combinatorial marker expression may correlate with the connectivity and cooperativity categories shown here.

span.label: cell-type labelling was verified in only one of the mouse lines, the rest taken on the strength of prior documentation
span.quote: Since the high reliability of cell-type specific labelling in the mouse lines used for cross-breeding has been documented before ( Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004 , Ma et al., 2006 , Oliva et al., 2000 , Pfeffer et al., 2013 , Sippy and Yuste, 2013 , Taniguchi et al., 2011 ), we only confirmed labelling in VIP-cre∷LSL-TOM with immunohistochemistry (86.3% of TOM cells were VIP-immunoreactive, while 94.9% of VIP-immunoreactive cells contained TOM).

span.label: the animals were naive, and other work suggests some of this wiring changes with learning
span.quote: While we used naïve mice in our experiments, other evidence suggest that VIPs and PVs can wire into a mutually inhibitory dyad during learning ( Donato et al., 2013 , David et al., 2007 ), which might also necessitate rewiring them to different excitatory sources.

span.label: the compartmentalisation of cooperativity into local teams is offered as a hypothesis for future study
span.quote: We hypothesize for further studies that the INs within a nearby volume of cortex and within one of these populations (IN team “A”) might be co-active/cooperative while another team “B” of the same population further away might be completely independent of team A’s actions. This type of compartmentalization may help regulate cooperativity so that all population members across the neocortex do not co-activate after some threshold is passed.

span.label: monosynaptic rabies tracing from genetically defined starter cells, used to ask how much local input each class receives
span.quote: To address this, we assessed the extent to which VIPs, compared to SOMs, are innervated by nearby PCs, by tracing presynaptic neurons of VIPs and SOMs with rabies (see Methods). Since similar experiments have been performed in V1

span.label: sequential stimulation of soma-sized volumes while recording two cells, to ask whether their inputs are shared
span.quote: Since these data suggest that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic partners, as a positive control we ran the same protocol on PVs. We chose PVs because they had the highest subthreshold cross-correlations in our data ( Figure S3C ), suggesting that they share many presynaptic partners

span.label: agonist and antagonist muscle pairs, used as the argument for why two mutually inhibitory populations should not share excitatory drive
span.quote: The situation is similar to motor coordination of agonist/antagonist muscle pairs where simultaneous contraction of both would not be energetically advantageous. Along this line of reasoning, it would make sense to segregate PC networks to feed only into one population of a mutually inhibitory pair of IN populations. Our data in Figures 3 and S3 support this hypothesis in the case of SOMs and VIPs.

span.label: co-activity of principal cells during ongoing activity, imported as the question to ask of inhibitory cells
span.quote: Co-activation of neurons inevitably depends on synaptic connectivity of excitatory as well as inhibitory neurons, but while co-activity of neocortical principal cells (PCs) has been studied extensively ( Ch’ng and Reid, 2010 , Miller et al., 2014 , Bathellier et al., 2012 , Sakata and Harris, 2009 ), that of inhibitory interneurons (INs) has received little attention.

span.label: running the identical protocol on PV cells, where shared presynaptic partners ARE expected
span.quote: Since these data suggest that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic partners, as a positive control we ran the same protocol on PVs.

span.label: comparing baseline firing rate between control and GABA receptor blockade - a manipulation check reported inside a parenthesis
span.quote: In this dataset the firing rate of the recorded SOMs increased 58 ± 16 % when the other 3 SOMs were induced to fire in control conditions (while baseline firing rates were similar in control, 1.9 ± 0.2 Hz and during GABA receptor blockade, 1.9 ± 0.3 Hz, P = 0.68).

span.label: inspecting active and passive electrophysiological properties of VIPs grouped by cooperativity and by their response to GABA blockade - the sentence states the check and not its result, so no outcome is recorded
span.quote: As this variation could be characteristic of putative subclasses of VIP cells ( Rudy et al., 2011 ), we inspected the active and passive electrophysiological properties of VIPs categorized by their cooperativity in control conditions or their change in cooperativity in response to GABA receptor blockers ( Figure S5 ).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Locomotion increased the pairwise correlations within both VIP (stationary R = 0.07 ± 0.01, locomotion R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038) and SOM populations (stationary R = 0.13 ± 0.04, locomotion R = 0.22 ± 0.04, P = 0.005), consistent with increased neuronal activity during animal movement.

span.label: locomotion
span.quote: Locomotion increased the pairwise correlations within both VIP (stationary R = 0.07 ± 0.01, locomotion R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038) and SOM populations (stationary R = 0.13 ± 0.04, locomotion R = 0.22 ± 0.04, P = 0.005), consistent with increased neuronal activity during animal movement.

span.label: THE EXPERIMENT THAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NAMED, AND THE REAGENT DOES NOT EXIST: suitable loss-of-function tests would need synaptic blockers simultaneously specific to both the presynaptic and the postsynaptic population, so the mechanisms are implied by correlation rather than directly
span.quote: We note however that as suitable loss-of-function experiments to test the contribution of these mechanisms to IN population co-activity do not yet exist (synaptic blockers simultaneously specific to both pre- and postsynaptic populations would be necessary), our data mostly imply the involvement of these mechanisms by correlation rather than directly.

span.label: and the single exception is marked as such - one figure directly demonstrates the GABAergic role in cooperative recruitment, and the paper says which one
span.quote: A key exception to this is shown in Figure 5D–E , which directly demonstrates the role of GABAergic inhibition in cooperative recruitment of SOMs.

span.label: A POSITIVE CONTROL CHOSEN ON THE STRENGTH OF AN EARLIER MEASUREMENT IN THE SAME DATASET: PVs are used to validate the shared-input assay because they had the highest subthreshold cross-correlations here, so they should share presynaptic partners
span.quote: Since these data suggest that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic partners, as a positive control we ran the same protocol on PVs. We chose PVs because they had the highest subthreshold cross-correlations in our data ( Figure S3C ), suggesting that they share many presynaptic partners

span.label: and the null is only interpretable because that control worked - shared inputs were detectable in PV pairs and indistinguishable from zero in VIP-SOM pairs
span.quote: The proportion of ‘shared’ L-EPSCs from all L-EPSCs can be interpreted as an approximation of the percentage of shared presynaptic cells between the two recorded neurons ( Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005 ). This proportion was 22.6 ± 5.6 % for PV-PV pairs and −0.8 ± 4.9 % for VIP-SOM pairs (P = 0.015, Figure 3H ). The latter was not significantly different from zero (z-test against zero, P = 0.95) implying that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic cells.

span.label: THE MEASURE IS BUILT BY SUBTRACTING THE BASELINE INTO EXISTENCE: laser-EPSCs are the post-stimulus count minus the pre-stimulus count, so the quantity itself is a difference and can legitimately come out negative
span.quote: To account for the baseline rate of spontaneous EPSCs, we also counted ‘shared’ and ‘not shared’ EPSCs during the 130 ms before each stimulus. For each neuron pair, total ‘not shared’ EPSC frequency increased from 18.7 ± 7.9 Hz before stimulus to 19.6 ± 7.9 Hz following stimulus (n = 6 cell pairs, paired T-test P = 0.008) indicating that the stimulation reliably recruited presynaptic excitatory neurons. However there was no significant change in shared EPSCs from before (0.34 ± 0.15 Hz) to after stimulation (0.35 ± 0.16 Hz, paired T-test P = 0.74). Within the categories ‘shared’ and ‘not shared’, we subtracted the spontaneous EPSC counts before stimuli from those following it to obtain a metric we call laser-EPSCs

span.label: the correlation analysis is repeated on binarized data specifically to avoid systematic biases in the fluorescence measure it was first computed on
span.quote: To avoid potential systematic biases in the ΔF/F correlations, we repeated the analyses with binarized data (see Methods) and obtained similar results

span.label: THE CATEGORIES ARE DECLARED CONVENIENT RATHER THAN FUNDAMENTAL: the three markers are used because transgenic lines exist for them, and further subpopulations are expected inside each
span.quote: While the IN populations can be conveniently categorized by the non-overlapping markers SOM, PV and VIP to utilize transgenic mice, we note that there are likely further subpopulations within these that should fit the cooperativity/co-activity framework described here on average for these broad populations. Although we did not find subdivisions that correlate with consistent differences in electrophysiological parameters ( Figure S5 ), other metrics such as combinatorial marker expression may correlate with the connectivity and cooperativity categories shown here.

span.label: AND THE UNIT OF COMPUTATION IS PROPOSED TO CHANGE: groups rather than individual neurons, and reciprocally inhibitory dyads rather than a sequential hierarchy
span.quote: We therefore propose an updated standard model for IN connectivity in the neocortex featuring reciprocally inhibitory population dyads rather than sequential hierarchy of populations and groups rather than individual neurons as computational units

span.label: a distance threshold is set from the data rather than chosen: correlations approach zero beyond 150 micrometres, which is read as the range over which inputs are shared and then used as the analysis cutoff
span.quote: All zero-offset correlation coefficients approached 0 at intersomatic distances above 150 mm ( Fig 3D ), suggesting that the correlation reflects shared synaptic inputs from nearby cells.

span.label: contradicts → Pfeffer et al. (2013) on target-selective inhibition by PV interneurons
span.quote: In contrast to previous findings ( Pfeffer et al., 2013 ), we find that PVs inhibit IN targets unselectively ( Figure 4A , S4 ).

span.label: extends → Hofer et al. (2011) on PV interneuron co-activity
span.quote: Here we showed that SOMs and VIPs demonstrate within-population co-activity ( Figure 1 , 5 ) on a timescale of hundreds of milliseconds, and previous work has shown that PVs act similarly ( Hofer et al., 2011 ).

span.label: replicates → Hu et al. (2011) and Ma et al. (2012) on the absence of SOM-to-SOM inhibition
span.quote: The lowest inhibitory connectivity rates were within SOMs (0%, in agreement with Hu et al., 2011 , Ma et al., 2012 ), within VIPs and from VIPs to PVs ( Figure S4 ).

span.label: contradicts → the prevailing hierarchical disinhibitory model built from activating one interneuron population at a time
span.quote: The inhibitory connectivity of PVs, SOMs and VIPs was recently described by optogenetically activating one population at a time ( Lee et al., 2013 , Pfeffer et al., 2013 , Pi et al., 2013 ) leading to a prevailing model of hierarchical disinhibitory motifs ( Hangya et al., 2014 , Harris and Shepherd, 2015 , Kepecs and Fishell, 2014 ). However, it is unclear how interneurons coordinate their activity within subpopulations. It is particularly puzzling how mutually inhibitory interneuron populations manage to operate together while embedded within a highly interconnected network

span.label: extends → the demonstration that parvalbumin interneurons are co-active during ongoing activity, generalised here to two more classes
span.quote: It is important to study co-activity patterns of other INs during ongoing activity, as it reflects flow of information through the cortical circuit without sensory driven thalamocortical input and is therefore the optimal situation to assess

span.label: qualifies → the account of VIP interneurons as specialists in long-range excitation, by showing comparable local input
span.quote: We counted starter and presynaptic cells at the injection site across 4 VIP-cre and 3 SOM-cre brains and found that VIPs and SOMs get input from nearby cells to a similar extent ( Figure 2E , VIPs: 93 ± 29 starters and 1259 ± 409 presynaptic cells/brain; SOMs: 118 ± 14 starters and 2535 ± 641 presynaptic cells/brain; P > 0.1). We annotated positions of labelled somata in the coronal sections and aligned these maps by the pial surface. The resulting average cell density heat maps ( Figure 2F , S2A,B ) indicate that both cell types receive input most heavily from L2/3.

span.label: supports → reports that within-population inhibition is absent among somatostatin cells
span.quote: The only population with high probability of within-population inhibition was PVs. The lowest inhibitory connectivity rates were within SOMs

span.label: qualifies → its own generalisation, since the mice were naive and some of this wiring is reported to change with learning
span.quote: While we used naïve mice in our experiments, other evidence suggest that VIPs and PVs can wire into a mutually inhibitory dyad during learning ( Donato et al., 2013 , David et al., 2007 ), which might also necessitate rewiring them to different excitatory sources.

span.label: VIP —distinct-from→ SOM
span.quote: Here we show in vivo and in vitro that members of two non-overlapping neocortical IN populations, expressing somatostatin (SOM) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), are active as populations rather than individually. We demonstrate a variety of synergistic mechanisms, involving population-specific local excitation, GABAergic disinhibition and excitation through electrical coupling, which likely underlie IN population co-activity. Firing of a few SOM or VIP INs recruits additional members within the cell type via GABAergic and cholinergic mechanisms, thereby amplifying the output of the population as a whole.

span.label: population —operationalised-as→ co-activ
span.quote: We first investigated spontaneous activity patterns of VIPs and SOMs by recording ongoing activity while mice were awake in a dark room. We used 2-photon Ca 2+ imaging through a thinned skull in primary visual cortex (V1) of VIP-cre∷LSL-TOM and SOM-cre∷LSL-TOM mice injected with AAV1-syn-GCAMP6s ( Figure 1 ). Both VIPs and SOMs were co-active with their population members

span.label: co-activ —part-of→ ongoing
span.quote: It is important to study co-activity patterns of other INs during ongoing activity, as it reflects flow of information through the cortical circuit without sensory driven thalamocortical input and is therefore the optimal situation to assess

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN IS A ROBUSTNESS CHECK REPORTING AGREEMENT) · correlation —distinct-from→ binarized
span.quote: To avoid potential systematic biases in the ΔF/F correlations, we repeated the analyses with binarized data (see Methods) and obtained similar results

span.label: shuffled —distinct-from→ co-activ
span.quote: We further analyzed the movies with highest amounts of GCAMP-expressing and active INs by counting how many INs were active together in the same frame in binarized data. This analysis also indicated that VIPs and SOMs are more co-active than shuffled surrogate data, or the other cells in the imaged region

span.label: locomotion —causes→ correlation
span.quote: Locomotion increased the pairwise correlations within both VIP (stationary R = 0.07 ± 0.01, locomotion R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038) and SOM populations (stationary R = 0.13 ± 0.04, locomotion R = 0.22 ± 0.04, P = 0.005), consistent with increased neuronal activity during animal movement.

span.label: locomotion —causes→ VIP
span.quote: Since activity of VIPs and SOMs is modulated by animal movement ( Fu et al., 2014 , Polack et al., 2013 ), we divided the data into ‘stationary’ and ‘locomotion’ epochs measured by monitoring movement of the running disk the mice were on.

span.label: depressing —contrasted-with→ facilitating
span.quote: PCs formed excitatory synapses onto VIPs and SOMs at similar rates, but synapses onto VIPs were depressing, while those onto SOMs were facilitating ( Figure 2A ). span.quote: This broad activation of the local microcircuit includes axon terminals expressing C1V1, therefore these results may be due to multiple complex network interactions among the excitatory and inhibitory cell types.

span.label: rabies —operationalised-as→ presynaptic
span.quote: To address this, we assessed the extent to which VIPs, compared to SOMs, are innervated by nearby PCs, by tracing presynaptic neurons of VIPs and SOMs with rabies (see Methods). Since similar experiments have been performed in V1

span.label: presynaptic —operationalised-as→ VIP
span.quote: We counted starter and presynaptic cells at the injection site across 4 VIP-cre and 3 SOM-cre brains and found that VIPs and SOMs get input from nearby cells to a similar extent ( Figure 2E , VIPs: 93 ± 29 starters and 1259 ± 409 presynaptic cells/brain; SOMs: 118 ± 14 starters and 2535 ± 641 presynaptic cells/brain; P > 0.1). The resulting average cell density heat maps ( Figure 2F , S2A,B ) indicate that both cell types receive input most heavily from L2/3.

span.label: spontaneous —operationalised-as→ presynaptic
span.quote: Out of 62 SOM activations recorded with another SOM, 55 % were shared; while out of 91 SOM or VIP activations (all recordings contained one SOM and one VIP) only 8.8 % were shared; and out of 25 VIP activations recorded with another VIP, 24 % were shared ( Figure 3B ). Shared VIP activations were rare probably since VIPs had an overall lower frequency of spontaneous activations (VIPs 0.0017 ± 0.0008 Hz, SOMs 0.0044 ± 0.0009 Hz). These data hint at a SOM specific excitatory presynaptic population.

span.label: intersomatic —causes→ correlation
span.quote: All zero-offset correlation coefficients approached 0 at intersomatic distances above 150 mm ( Fig 3D ), suggesting that the correlation reflects shared synaptic inputs from nearby cells.

span.label: correlation —operationalised-as→ PCs
span.quote: Correlation coefficients were not significantly different (P > 0.4) between SOM-SOM (0.054 ± 0.012, n = 13, intersomatic distance 57.4 ± 10.7 µm), VIP-PV (0.053 ± 0.016, n = 5, distance 56.9 ± 17.4 µm) and VIP-VIP pairs (0.041 ± 0.013, n = 11, distance 61.6 ± 11.9 µm). However VIP-SOM pairs had significantly lower correlations than all other pairs (0.014 ± 0.006, n = 18, P < 0.05, distance 61.8 ± 10.1 µm), supporting the notion that VIPs and SOMs are innervated by distinct sets of PCs.

span.label: positive control —operationalised-as→ PV
span.quote: Since these data suggest that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic partners, as a positive control we ran the same protocol on PVs. We chose PVs because they had the highest subthreshold cross-correlations in our data ( Figure S3C ), suggesting that they share many presynaptic partners

span.label: L-EPSC —operationalised-as→ PV
span.quote: PV-PV pairs (n = 5) had 201 ± 96.0 ‘not shared’ L-EPSCs (z-test against zero, P = 0.036) and 36.4 ± 8.6 ‘shared’ L-EPSCs (z-test against zero, P = 0.00002) indicating that both common and unique inputs were recruited by the laser stimulation

This proportion was 22.6 ± 5.6 % for PV-PV pairs and −0.8 ± 4.9 % for VIP-SOM pairs (P = 0.015, Figure 3H ). The latter was not significantly different from zero (z-test against zero, P = 0.95) implying that VIPs and SOMs do not share presynaptic cells.

span.label: subnetwork —part-of→ excitat
span.quote: In aggregate, the data in Figures 3 and S3 suggest that SOMs and VIPs are innervated at least in part by non-overlapping excitatory subnetworks.

span.quote: While the IN populations can be conveniently categorized by the non-overlapping markers SOM, PV and VIP to utilize transgenic mice, we note that there are likely further subpopulations within these that should fit the cooperativity/co-activity framework described here on average for these broad populations. Although we did not find subdivisions that correlate with consistent differences in electrophysiological parameters ( Figure S5 ), other metrics such as combinatorial marker expression may correlate with the connectivity and cooperativity categories shown here.

span.label: labelling —operationalised-as→ VIP

span.quote: Locomotion increased the pairwise correlations within both VIP (stationary R = 0.07 ± 0.01, locomotion R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038) and SOM populations (stationary R = 0.13 ± 0.04, locomotion R = 0.22 ± 0.04, P = 0.005), consistent with increased neuronal activity during animal movement.

span.label: ~85% — share of neocortical interneurons covered by the three non-overlapping PV, SOM and VIP populations
span.quote: PVs, together with somatostatin expressing cells (SOMs) and vasoactive intestinal peptide expressing cells (VIPs) form three non-overlapping populations that account for ~85% of neocortical INs ( Rudy et al., 2011 )

span.label: 68%, 8643/12641 cells — proportion of rabies-labelled presynaptic cells with clear pyramidal morphology
span.quote: Most presynaptic cells (68%, 8643/12641 cells) had clear pyramidal morphology ( Figure 2D )

span.label: 68 ± 22 % — increase in spontaneous firing of the fourth SOM when three other SOMs were driven to fire
span.quote: Driving three SOM cells to fire was sufficient to significantly increase firing in the fourth SOM (68 ± 22 % increase in spontaneous firing, n = 13, Figure 5B ), demonstrating within-population recruitment.

span.label: 22.6 ± 5.6 % vs −0.8 ± 4.9 % — estimated proportion of shared presynaptic cells for PV-PV pairs versus VIP-SOM pairs
span.quote: This proportion was 22.6 ± 5.6 % for PV-PV pairs and −0.8 ± 4.9 % for VIP-SOM pairs (P = 0.015, Figure 3H ).

span.label: R = 0.07 ± 0.01 to R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038 — rise in within-VIP pairwise correlation from stationary to locomotion epochs
span.quote: Locomotion increased the pairwise correlations within both VIP (stationary R = 0.07 ± 0.01, locomotion R = 0.13 ± 0.03, P = 0.038) and SOM populations (stationary R = 0.13 ± 0.04, locomotion R = 0.22 ± 0.04, P = 0.005), consistent with increased neuronal activity during animal movement.

span.label: 86.3% / 94.9% — specificity and sensitivity of the VIP-cre reporter line checked by immunohistochemistry
span.quote: we only confirmed labelling in VIP-cre∷LSL-TOM with immunohistochemistry (86.3% of TOM cells were VIP-immunoreactive, while 94.9% of VIP-immunoreactive cells contained TOM).

span.label: 55 % / 8.8 % / 24 % — share of spontaneous depolarizing activations shared within SOM pairs, across SOM-VIP pairs, and within VIP pairs
span.quote: Out of 62 SOM activations recorded with another SOM, 55 % were shared; while out of 91 SOM or VIP activations (all recordings contained one SOM and one VIP) only 8.8 % were shared; and out of 25 VIP activations recorded with another VIP, 24 % were shared ( Figure 3B ).

span.label: 16 ± 7 %, P = 0.007 — residual SOM firing-rate increase surviving GABA-A and GABA-B receptor blockade
span.quote: This increase was significantly reduced to 16 ± 7 % during GABA receptor blockade (n = 7, paired t-test P = 0.007, Figure 5D,E ), indicating that disinhibition of SOMs by SOMs is an important mechanism for their cooperative recruitment.

span.label: 150 mm — the intersomatic distance beyond which subthreshold correlations vanish, read from the data and then used as the analysis cutoff
span.quote: All zero-offset correlation coefficients approached 0 at intersomatic distances above 150 mm ( Fig 3D ), suggesting that the correlation reflects shared synaptic inputs from nearby cells.

span.label: 86.3% — labelled cells that were immunoreactive in the one line checked, against 94.9 percent the other way
span.quote: Since the high reliability of cell-type specific labelling in the mouse lines used for cross-breeding has been documented before ( Chattopadhyaya et al., 2004 , Ma et al., 2006 , Oliva et al., 2000 , Pfeffer et al., 2013 , Sippy and Yuste, 2013 , Taniguchi et al., 2011 ), we only confirmed labelling in VIP-cre∷LSL-TOM with immunohistochemistry (86.3% of TOM cells were VIP-immunoreactive, while 94.9% of VIP-immunoreactive cells contained TOM).

span.label: 55 % — spontaneous activations shared within a class, against 8.8 percent across the two
span.quote: Out of 62 SOM activations recorded with another SOM, 55 % were shared; while out of 91 SOM or VIP activations (all recordings contained one SOM and one VIP) only 8.8 % were shared; and out of 25 VIP activations recorded with another VIP, 24 % were shared ( Figure 3B ). Shared VIP activations were rare probably since VIPs had an overall lower frequency of spontaneous activations (VIPs 0.0017 ± 0.0008 Hz, SOMs 0.0044 ± 0.0009 Hz). These data hint at a SOM specific excitatory presynaptic population.

span.label: 26 ± 7 Hz — average firing rate SOMs ramped up to during the light pulse, while VIPs tended to fire a single AP at the beginning followed by quiescence
span.quote: VIPs and SOMs were recruited in a highly stereotyped manner during optogenetic activation; VIPs tended to fire a single AP in the beginning of the 0.5 s light pulse, followed by quiescence, while SOMs ramped up to an average firing rate of 26 ± 7 Hz during the pulse
